It calls on the federal court system to bar construction before it starts.
Otherwise, the lawsuit warns, Trump could claim that pausing construction already under way would pose a national security risk, as he has done with other controversial projects in the past.
“This is not the first time that Defendants have rushed to dramatically remake the District too quickly for courts to intervene,” the lawsuit reads. “This Court should not allow this effort to escape judicial scrutiny.”
Saturday’s complaint brings the total number of lawsuits against the arch to three.
Trump has championed the prospect of building a triumphal arch, similar to the Arc de Triomphe built in Paris during Napoleonic times.
Trump’s arch, however, is designed to stand 30 metres (100 feet) taller than the Statue of Liberty. It would tower from the Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, at 76 metres (250ft).
That colossal scale has prompted outrage, particularly from veterans’ groups who fear the arch would block views of Arlington National Cemetery, a hallowed military grave site.
White House officials maintain that ground could be broken as early as next week, on or around November 5.
On Friday, the administration unveiled a 106-page proposal for the arch to be a 12-storey megastructure, featuring a winged bronze statue of Lady Liberty lifting an eternal flame.
The arch would include two mezzanines and an observation deck with panoramic east-west views, as well as programme spaces, offices and a “fire command centre”.
Trump has previously said the arch would double as a military hub with snipers and drone capabilities.
Construction on the arch would also result in significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic to nearby roads.
In Saturday’s lawsuit, Attorneys General Brian Schwalb of Washington, DC, and Jay Jones of Virginia pointed to the project’s disruptive footprint as a major concern.
“As soon as defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia,” the lawsuit said.
It warns that the anticipated three-year construction project will stymie commuter traffic, slow down emergency vehicles and generate significant pollution, including “stormwater runoff into the Potomac”.
The lawsuit calls on the court to force the Trump administration to get congressional authorisation before any construction can begin.
The new legal challenge comes on the heels of an October 8 filing by Arlington County, which was the first governmental body to mount a legal action against Trump’s planned monument.
In that lawsuit, the county’s governing board argued that the project would cause “significant harm” to its residents and likely require changes to nearby flight paths.
The first complaint came in February, when a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian launched an effort to stop the arch.
District Judge Tanya Chutkan is overseeing that case, and she is weighing whether to issue a preliminary injunction to temporarily freeze any construction plans while the court hears arguments.
At a hearing on Friday, Chutkan deferred an immediate ruling but signalled that she would be issuing a decision expeditiously.
She previously ordered the administration to give the court 48 hours’ notice before undertaking any activities related to the construction of the arch.
The monument has already received early approval from the US Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump.

A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar
- Summary:
- A computer scientist has achieved a breakthrough in a nearly 25-year-old problem involving how computers calculate distances across enormous networks. The new algorithm delivers more reliable estimates for closely connected points without sacrificing speed, overcoming a longstanding limitation of earlier methods. Its secret lies in a smarter way of sampling network connections at multiple scales.
- Share:
Finding the shortest route between two locations is something navigation apps like Google Maps do every day. Behind the scenes, sophisticated algorithms analyze networks of roads and intersections to identify efficient paths. But what if a computer needed to calculate the shortest distance between every possible pair of locations in an enormous network?
That challenge extends far beyond maps. Similar calculations are important for transportation systems, communication networks, and even biological structures involving proteins, neurons, or other interconnected components. As these networks grow, determining the shortest routes between all their points becomes increasingly difficult.
Computer scientists call this the All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) problem. It involves finding the shortest distance between every pair of points in a graph. In this context, a 'graph' is simply a collection of points (called vertices) joined by connections (called edges). Those points might represent cities, PCs, subway stations, or organs, while the connections could stand for highways, cables, railway lines, or blood vessels.
Why Calculating Shortest Paths Is So Difficult
Determining the exact shortest distances across a massive network can consume enormous amounts of computing time and memory. In densely connected networks, some conventional approaches require what mathematicians call cubic time. That means doubling the number of points can increase the computational workload by roughly eight times.
Because the required computation (work) can grow much faster than the network itself, researchers have spent decades searching for more efficient methods. One promising solution is to use approximation algorithms, which calculate estimates rather than exact answers. The goal is to produce distances that are sufficiently accurate while dramatically reducing the amount of computation required.
An important advance came in 1996, when researchers Dor, Halperin, and Zwick (DHZ) developed a method capable of producing distance estimates within twice the actual shortest distance for sufficiently distant points, while operating in nearly optimal time.
This level of accuracy is known as a "2‑approximation." For example, if the shortest possible route between two locations is 10 kilometers, an estimate satisfying this guarantee would fall between 10 and 20 kilometers.
Rather than examining every possible route, the DHZ approach uses a relatively small selection of points from the network (referred to as sampled vertices). These strategically selected points serve as shortcuts that help the algorithm estimate distances more efficiently.
A Clever Shortcut With a Hidden Weakness
The approach works particularly well when the points being compared are far apart.
Consider a journey between Delhi and Chennai. Because the cities are separated by a considerable distance, the algorithm can often find a sampled point close to the shortest route. This allows it to calculate an estimate that remains within the promised limit of twice the actual distance.
However, the same strategy becomes less dependable when the two points are close together.
Imagine calculating the shortest route between two neighborhoods in the Mumbai suburbs. The sampled points might be located too far from the most direct connection, forcing the algorithm to estimate a much longer route.
For example, two points might be connected by a path containing just two edges, yet the sampled route could contain five. Because five exceeds twice the true distance of two, the result violates the "at most twice" accuracy guarantee.
This weakness meant that the original algorithm's mathematical guarantee applied only when the points were sufficiently far apart. For closer connections, the same level of accuracy could not always be assured.
That limitation remained a challenge for nearly three decades.
A New Algorithm Breaks Through a Decades-Old Limit
Now, Dr. Manoj Gupta, an Associate Professor at the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar, has introduced a refinement that extends the accuracy guarantee to points much closer together than earlier methods allowed.

Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University of Birmingham
- Summary:
- Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.
- Share:
What if time is not a fundamental part of the universe, but something that emerges from the changes taking place inside it? A physicist at the University of Birmingham has created a miniature universe in the laboratory that offers a surprising new way to investigate this possibility.
Using thousands of atoms cooled to temperatures barely above absolute zero, Professor Giovanni Barontini demonstrated that the passage of time can be measured without relying on an external clock. Instead, a form of time emerges naturally from the behavior of particles within the experimental system.
The findings, published in Physical Review Research, provide experimental evidence for an intriguing idea in theoretical physics: Time may not be an essential ingredient of reality. It could arise from the relationships and changes occurring within the universe itself.
Why Some Physicists Think Time May Not Be Fundamental
We usually think of time as something that continuously moves forward, regardless of what happens around us. Seconds pass, planets orbit stars, and the universe evolves. But some theories of physics suggest that time may work very differently at the most fundamental level.
One example is the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, which appears in attempts to combine quantum mechanics with gravity. In this framework, the universe can be described as a single, unchanging quantum state, with no external clock marking the passage of time. Quantum particles can exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties, but the universe as a whole does not necessarily have a built-in time variable.
This creates a major puzzle. If the universe has no external clock, how can anything happen in a particular order? What determines which events come first and which happen later?
One possibility is that time emerges from the changing relationships between different parts of the universe. Barontini designed an experiment to investigate whether such a process could be observed in the laboratory.
Creating a Miniature Universe With 24,000 Atoms
To build his miniature cosmos, Barontini used a cloud of approximately 24,000 atoms cooled to just a few billionths of a degree above absolute zero. At these extraordinarily low temperatures, quantum effects become especially important, allowing researchers to study behaviors that are normally difficult to observe.
The atoms were confined inside a carefully controlled quantum system designed to remain isolated from its surroundings. Two laser beams operating at different frequencies created a thin barrier that divided the system into two regions: an observed ('bright') region and an unobserved ('dark') region.
Although the overall system was isolated from the outside world, atoms could move between these two regions.
The bright region underwent repeated cycles of expansion and contraction, resembling simplified versions of two dramatic cosmological events. The expansion was analogous to the Big Bang, while the contraction resembled a Big Crunch, a hypothetical fate of the universe in which cosmic expansion eventually reverses and everything collapses inward.
The experiment did not recreate these actual cosmic events. Instead, it provided a simplified quantum model in which researchers could investigate how a sequence of events might be reconstructed without referring to a clock outside the system.
How Time Emerged Without a Clock
The key to the experiment was entropy, a concept in physics associated with the spread or disorder (entropy) of particles and energy.
Rather than using seconds or minutes, Barontini developed a way to track time through changes in how atoms were distributed within the miniature universe.
As atoms moved between the bright and dark regions, the distribution of particles in the bright region changed. These changes provided a way to define the system's progression through time, even when the bright region alternated between expansion and contraction.
When the particle distribution increased or decreased in its spread, the system continued moving forward according to this internal measure of time. When the distribution remained unchanged, the progression of this particular form of time effectively stopped.

with Knowledge Graphs: A Production

sources.title:
How to Detect Financial Fraud Patterns
with Knowledge Graphs: A Production
Guide
sources.text:
Most anti-fraud architectures in enterprise payment workflows evaluate transactions in isolation.
When an invoice arrives, an automated rules engine checks it against static thresholds. It checks whether the dollar amount falls within normal limits, whether the vendor is on an approved vendor list, and whether the submitting IP address looks familiar. If the individual attributes look plausible, the payment clears.
The problem with this approach is structural. Sophisticated fraud schemes like money mule rings, circular invoicing loops, and vendor collision rarely produce transactions that alert individual thresholds. A shell company invoicing $4,800 to stay under a $5,000 dual sign-off threshold looks completely fine in isolation. But when 25 seemingly independent vendors all route disbursements to the same bank account, the coordinated pattern starts to become clear.
You won't find the warning in the attributes of an isolated transaction. It lives in the topology of the payment network.
In a relational database, tracing these multi-entity relationships requires recursive cell joins across tables of vendors, invoices, payments, and bank accounts. But as tables grow into millions of rows, deep path traversals quickly degrade query performance. Graph databases solve this by storing relationships as first-class, index-free adjacency pointers, turning multi-hop traversals into constant-time lookups.
In this tutorial, you'll explore the architecture of an end-to-end relational fraud detection pipeline built on Neo4j. You'll see how to model financial entities as a graph, precompute derived edges to optimize query latency, and write parameterized Cypher queries to uncover five core procurement fraud schemes.
The complete reference implementation is available in the fraud-detection-knowledge-graphs repository.
In accounts payable pipelines, risk checks typically operate on isolated records:
# Transaction-level view — nothing suspicious
transactions = [
{"vendor": "Alpha Corp", "amount": 5200.00, "date": "2025-08-01"},
{"vendor": "Beta LLC", "amount": 4800.00, "date": "2025-08-02"},
{"vendor": "Gamma Inc", "amount": 5100.00, "date": "2025-08-03"},
]
# All amounts within normal range ($1K–$15K). All vendors valid.
# Dates are sequential. Nothing triggers any rule.
When you map those same records to an interconnected graph, the hidden structure becomes clear right away:
# Graph view — all three vendors pay to the same account
connections = {
"ACC-MULE-001": ["Alpha Corp", "Beta LLC", "Gamma Inc"],
"ACC-0042": ["Delta Corp", "Epsilon LLC"],
"ACC-0099": ["Zeta GmbH"],
}
# ACC-MULE-001 receives from 25+ vendors. That's a money mule ring.
# The convergence is the red flag.
The underlying data hasn't changed. But when you evaluate transactions within an entity graph, the coordinated funnel stands out.
In a relational database, connecting these dots requires multiple joins across separate table. In a knowledge graph, the connections are stored directly as edges connecting nodes, which allows you to query them in a single traversal.
| Pattern | What It Is | What Traditional Tools Don't Catch |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate Invoices | Same invoice and vendor, near-identical amount, close dates | Exact match misses slight variations |
| Circular Rings | Vendors invoicing each other in a closed loop | Each invoice looks legitimate alone |
| Money Mule Rings | Many vendors funneling to one controlled account | No single payment is anomalous |
| Vendor Collusion | Independent-looking vendors sharing underlying attributes | No cluster detection across entities |
| Payment Anomalies | Invoice approved by someone outside their department's authority | Role-based checks pass, context checks don't exist |
A knowledge graph doesn't replace rules engines or ML models. But it does fill the gap they can't reach: relationships.

Before running fraud queries, you need to structure your data into a cohesive property graph. The reference dataset models six entity types commonly found in financial systems:
| Entity | Key Properties | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Vendor | tax_id, name, country, city | Who issues invoices |
| Invoice | invoice_id, amount, date, category | What was billed |
| Payment | payment_id, amount, date | What was paid |
| BankAccount | account_id, routing_number, bank_name | Where money went |
| Employee | employee_id, name, department | Who approved |
| Organization | org_id, name, departments | Structural hierarchy |
The base relationships form a bipartite payment network:
(Employee)-[:APPROVED]->(Payment)-[:LINKED_TO]->(Invoice)-[:ISSUED_BY]->(Vendor)
|

(Payment)-[:PAID_TO]->(BankAccount)
